extracted.intended_audience: aspiring fiction writers and authors learning narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and examples for recognizing and crafting unreliable narrators in fiction (including novels, short stories, film, and children’s books). Focuses on the narrative features that make a voice untrustworthy and the effects those choices produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of unreliable narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: A character who may not provide a completely accurate or trustworthy account of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page opens with this working definition: their perspective might be skewed and they might leave out crucial details, leading readers to question the truth of the narrative. This baseline frames all subsequent examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skewed perspective and omission of crucial details
rubrics_metrics.description: Narration that is colored or selective — the narrator leaves out or downplays important facts, producing a distorted account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the article notes unreliable narrators 'may leave out crucial details' and that selective memory contributes to uncertainty (cited in Holden Caulfield). Use omission to invite readers to doubt and piece together the truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional turmoil that clouds judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator whose emotional instability (grief, rage, teenage angst, etc.) makes their telling subjective and unreliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Holden Caulfield — 'emotional turmoil and selective memory' cloud judgment and memory. Guidance: show the narrator's strong emotions and let those emotions skew perception rather than presenting dispassionate facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator bias and subjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Narration shaped by the narrator’s personal biases, social or cultural perspective, or ideological stance, which warps interpretation of events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Marlow in Heart of Darkness — 'biased storytelling and subjective interpretation' raise questions about reliability. Use internal assumptions, prejudice, or cultural blind spots to make the voice untrustworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate manipulation and hidden agendas
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator who intentionally deceives, manipulates readers, or hides motives, producing false or misleading accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Amy Dunne in Gone Girl — 'manipulative nature and hidden agenda' create plot twists. Guidance: crafted unreliability can be an intentional technique to surprise or mislead readers; keep internal logic consistent even when actions deceive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory gaps caused by substance abuse or trauma
rubrics_metrics.description: Narration fragmented by alcoholism, drug use, or trauma that produces lapses, missing time, or unreliable recollections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Rachel Watson in The Girl on the Train — 'struggle with alcoholism leads to memory gaps and unreliable recollections.' Use gaps to create suspense and force readers to infer what actually happened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amnesia / fragmented memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrator suffers memory loss (partial or total) producing a fractured, fragmentary account of events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cadence in We Were Liars (memory loss after an accident); Leonard in Memento (anterograde amnesia). The article highlights 'fragmented and often unreliable narrative' and shows how the fractured memory becomes a structural device for mystery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental illness, psychological distress, and descent into madness
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychological instability, delusions, hallucinations, or mania that distort perception and narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Tell-Tale Heart's unnamed narrator ('descent into madness results in distorted perceptions'); Black Swan's Nina Sayers ('grapples with her sanity'). Use interior signs of instability (obsession, guilt, hallucination) to call factual accuracy into question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonlinear or structurally disorienting narrative devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of reversed chronology, fragmentation, or other formal structures that mirror or create unreliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Memento uses a non-linear reverse-chronological structure to make the audience experience the protagonist’s unreliable perspective. The article notes that structure itself can be a tool to 'add an element of confusion' and make readers piece the plot together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withholding information / silence as a device
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator who withholds facts, refuses to speak, or leaves clues (diaries, silence) rather than offering a full account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Alicia Berenson in The Silent Patient — 'has not spoken' and leaves a mysterious diary. The article shows silence/omission can propel suspense and create an investigative dynamic for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confessional or first-person obsession
rubrics_metrics.description: An intimate first-person confession that centers subjective feeling and rationalization, often justifying or reinterpreting questionable acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Poe’s unnamed narrator is a confession driven by obsession and guilt. The piece highlights that confessional tone can heighten unreliability by focusing on inner justification rather than objective description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple perspectives and competing accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Using more than one narrator or perspective so that accounts clash and truth becomes ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The Girl on the Train's multi-perspective structure 'weaves a web of truths and deceptions.' The article suggests contrasting viewpoints can magnify uncertainty and force readers to triangulate truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unusual or non-human narrators with interpretive bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrators who are non-human or otherwise unusual voices (e.g., Death) bring unique assumptions and a specific interpretive lens that makes the telling partial or stylized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Death in The Book Thief — 'Death’s observations and interpretation of events add an intriguing layer.' Guidance: such voices offer perspective but also their own limitations and agendas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Childlike imagination and fantasy that blur reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Narration shaped by a child’s imagination or fantastical framing where internal fantasy world and external reality are intermixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Max in Where the Wild Things Are and Alice in Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland — imaginative perception 'blurs the boundaries between fantasy and reality' and creates playful or unsettling unreliability. Useful in children’s literature to explore identity and perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose & effects of using an unreliable narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: Using unreliability to add depth, intrigue, suspense, and to challenge readers’ perception of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article repeatedly notes that unreliable narrators 'add depth and intrigue,' 'make readers question the truth,' 'build suspense,' and 'engage you in a unique reading experience.' When crafting an unreliable voice, keep in mind these intended effects and use unreliability deliberately to serve theme, tension, or character insight.
